title: Hubble/Chandra/Spitzer composite image of NGC 602, in the “wing” of the Small Magellanic Cloud
caption: The star cluster NGC 602 in the Wing of the Small Magellanic Cloud, imaged by Chandra, Hubble and Spitzer
credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/Univ.Potsdam/L.Oskinova et al; Optical: ESA, NASA/STScI; Infrared: NASA/JPL-Caltech

recognition.text: Published in the ESA/Hubble image archive. No published rating.

story: This composite from NASA's Great Observatories shows the cluster NGC 602 and its surroundings in the Wing, a region of the Small Magellanic Cloud, which orbits the Milky Way. Chandra's X-ray data appear in purple, Hubble's visible light in red, green and blue, and Spitzer's infrared data in red.

Chandra made the first detection of X-rays from young Sun-like stars outside our galaxy here. X-rays from young stars reveal how active their magnetic fields are, and magnetic activity offers clues to how fast a star spins and how hot gas rises and falls inside it.

Astronomers suggest that if young stars have similar X-ray properties in very different environments, then related properties, such as how planets form around them, are likely to be similar too. Studying young stars in another galaxy therefore helps astronomers test whether stars and planets form the same way in very different surroundings.

understand.summary: The image combines Chandra X-rays (shown in purple), Hubble Advanced Camera for Surveys visible and hydrogen-alpha light (in red, green and blue), and Spitzer IRAC infrared data (in red).
understand.eye: X-rays and infrared light are both invisible to the eye, so much of this picture shows light we could never see directly.
